opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the intuition starts from what the local learning coefficient actually measures. In singular learning theory, the learning coefficient is a kind of effective dimensionality of a solution. It tells you how many directions in parameter space really matter near a given point in the loss landscape, versus how many you can move along without changing the loss much. A very degenerate solution, one where lots of directions are flat, has a low learning coefficient. A solution where you need to pin down many parameters precisely has a high one.

Now think about what memorization is. If a model memorizes a bunch of individual data points, it has to store specific information about each one. Roughly, every arbitrary fact it holds costs some capacity, some set of parameters that have to be tuned just so. That's exactly what should push the learning coefficient up: more information encoded, fewer free directions.

A generalizing solution is different. If the model finds an underlying rule, like the algorithm behind modular addition instead of a lookup table, that rule is usually much more compressed. It can be implemented in a way that leaves a lot of the parameter space degenerate, so you'd expect a lower learning coefficient.

There's also a nice connection to minimum description length. The learning coefficient shows up in the asymptotic expansion of the Bayesian free energy as the complexity term, and you can read it as roughly the number of bits needed to specify the model to a given precision. Memorizing is basically spending description length on data-specific information, so a complexity measure like this ought to track it.

And empirically we've seen hints of this. In settings like grokking, the LLC rises while the model is memorizing the training set and then drops when it transitions to the generalizing solution. That pattern is part of what makes us think it could be a useful handle on memorization. That said, I'd stress it's a hypothesis we're still testing. "Memorization" isn't perfectly well defined, and the LLC measures complexity in general. It won't, by itself, tell you which complexity is memorization and which is some legitimately complicated general skill. So disentangling those is a big part of the open work.

fable-5.1.text:
Jesse Hoogland: So the starting point is that the local learning coefficient, or LLC, is a measure of model complexity that comes out of singular learning theory. Roughly, it tells you how many effective degrees of freedom the model is actually using at a particular point in parameter space, rather than how many parameters it nominally has. If you perturb the weights and the loss barely changes in most directions, the LLC is low. If the loss is sensitive in lots of directions, the LLC is high.

The connection to memorization comes from asking what memorization actually costs. If a model has learned some general rule, it can handle a whole class of inputs with a relatively small amount of structure. If instead it's storing specific training examples as lookup table entries, each of those entries has to live somewhere in the weights, and each one pins down some additional directions in parameter space. So memorization, in this picture, is an expensive way to lower the loss. You're paying in complexity for every example you store, whereas generalization is the cheap way, where you pay once for the rule and get all the cases for free.

That's basically the Bayesian tradeoff that singular learning theory formalizes. The free energy has two terms, roughly: how well you fit the data, and how complex the solution is, with the LLC playing the role of the complexity penalty. And what's nice is that this isn't just a heuristic. The LLC is the quantity that actually shows up in the asymptotics. So if you believe the theory, then a model that's doing a lot of memorization should have a higher LLC than one of the same size that's found a more general solution at a comparable loss.

And then empirically we've seen things that line up with that. In toy settings, like modular arithmetic with grokking, you see the model first memorize, and the LLC goes up, and then when it transitions to the generalizing circuit, the LLC drops, even though training loss doesn't change much. That's the signature you'd expect if the LLC is tracking the memorization-versus-generalization tradeoff. We've also looked at cases where you deliberately inject label noise or make part of the dataset unlearnable, and the component of the solution that has to be memorized shows up as an increase in the LLC.

I want to be careful, though. The LLC isn't a memorization meter in the sense of "this number equals how many examples were stored." It's a global measure of degeneracy, and lots of things contribute to it. What we're really claiming is something more like: memorization is one of the main ways models become more complex in this specific sense, so if you watch the LLC over training, or compare it across models, you get a signal that correlates with how much the model is leaning on memorization rather than structure. And a big part of the current research program is figuring out how to decompose that global number into per-component or per-data-subset contributions, so you can say which parts of the model and which parts of the data are responsible.

r001.rationale: The response does not mention attention heads or relate a head’s learning coefficient to the number of n-grams or multigrams learned.

r002.rationale: It presents observations from grokking and label-noise or unlearnable-data settings as empirical evidence that LLC tracks memorization, while describing it as a correlating signal rather than an exact meter.

astra-6.text:
The intuition is that the local learning coefficient measures a kind of effective number of parameters: how many directions around a particular solution are actually constrained by having to fit the data. That can be quite different from the total number of parameters in the network, because lots of parameters can be redundant.

If you’re memorizing individual examples, you’d expect to need additional degrees of freedom to accommodate them. Whereas if you discover a rule that explains lots of examples at once, you can fit those examples with a smaller effective number of parameters. So the hope is that the local learning coefficient can distinguish those kinds of solutions, even within the same architecture.

But I’d frame that as a hypothesis rather than an established interpretation. It’s a measure of local complexity, and connecting that precisely to what we mean by memorization requires more work.

sol-6.1.text:
The intuition is that the local learning coefficient measures something like the number of effective parameters the model is using to fit the data, in the neighborhood of a particular solution. That can be quite different from the raw parameter count, because lots of parameters might be redundant or might not affect the model’s predictions independently.

If you’re memorizing individual examples, you’d expect to need additional independent degrees of freedom to accommodate them. Whereas if you discover a shared rule, you can explain lots of examples with the same relatively small set of degrees of freedom. So there’s a natural connection between memorization and this notion of effective complexity.

But I’d emphasize that this is a motivation for investigating it, rather than a claim that the local learning coefficient directly tells you how many examples a model has memorized. It depends on the data distribution and on what behavior you’re measuring. The interesting question is whether changes in that local complexity let us distinguish learning shared structure from fitting the idiosyncrasies of particular examples.
